stem: A 66-year-old man with Parkinson disease takes pramipexole three times daily. Because his tremor bothers him, he doubles the dose on his own without telling his physician. A week later his wife says he talks to people who are not in the room.
oneliner: 66M + Parkinson disease on pramipexole + doubled his dose on his own + a week later talks to people who are not there → which adverse effect?
ask: Which of the following adverse effects is he most likely having?

whyNot.A: Not the typical effect of **excess dopaminergic stimulation**
whyNot.B: The tremor would **improve** with more dopamine agonist

answer: Hallucinations and psychosis from excess dopamine agonist
why: **Too much dopaminergic stimulation (pramipexole, ropinirole, bromocriptine, levodopa) causes hallucinations and psychosis**, along with impulse-control problems and sleep attacks.

drug.name: Pramipexole (dopamine agonists)
drug.watch: Hallucinations, impulse-control disorders (gambling), sleep attacks, orthostatic hypotension, nausea

stem: A 26-year-old woman with generalized epilepsy has been seizure-free for 3 years on valproic acid. She plans to become pregnant and asks when in pregnancy the drug would pose the greatest risk to the fetus, since she would stop taking it as soon as the test is positive.
oneliner: 26F + generalized epilepsy on valproic acid + planning pregnancy + would stop it when pregnancy test turns positive → when is the fetal risk highest?
ask: Exposure during which of the following periods carries the greatest risk of fetal malformation?

whyNot.C: Mainly affects **growth and function**, not malformation
whyNot.D: Risk is mostly **neonatal adaptation**, not structural defects
whyNot.E: Risk is **neonatal sedation or withdrawal**, not malformation

answer: Weeks 3 to 8 (neural tube closure and organogenesis)
why: **Valproate** most often causes **neural tube defects**, and the **neural tube closes in weeks 3 to 4**; organogenesis runs through week 8. A positive test comes **too late**, so counseling happens **before conception** with folate.

drug.name: Valproic acid
drug.how: Blocks sodium channels and increases GABA
drug.use: Generalized and absence seizures, bipolar disorder, migraine prophylaxis
drug.watch: Neural tube defects (spina bifida), hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, tremor, weight gain, alopecia, thrombocytopenia

stem: A 42-year-old woman with focal seizures has taken carbamazepine for 9 years. She now has diffuse bone pain and weakness when climbing stairs. Calcium and phosphate are low-normal, alkaline phosphatase is raised and 25-hydroxyvitamin D is low. Her diet, sun exposure, renal function and fat absorption are normal.
oneliner: 42F + focal seizures on carbamazepine 9 y + bone pain, proximal weakness + high ALP, low 25-OH vit D + normal diet, sun, kidneys, gut → mechanism?
ask: Which mechanism best explains her low vitamin D?

options.B: Binding of vitamin D in the gut lumen
options.D: Poor dietary intake of vitamin D
options.E: Induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes that break down vitamin D

whyNot.A: **Renal conversion** to 1,25-OH D; the low level here is 25-OH D, and renal function is normal
whyNot.B: **Bile acid sequestrants** do this; the stem says fat absorption is normal
whyNot.D: **Diet and sun exposure** are stated to be normal

answer: Induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes that break down vitamin D
why: **Long-term carbamazepine + low 25-OH vitamin D with normal diet and sun** = **CYP450 induction speeds vitamin D breakdown**, causing osteomalacia.

drug.name: Carbamazepine
drug.how: Blocks voltage-gated Na+ channels, prolonging inactivation
drug.use: Focal seizures, trigeminal neuralgia, bipolar disorder
drug.watch: CYP450 inducer, SIADH and hyponatremia, agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia, SJS with HLA-B*1502, teratogen

stem: A 44-year-old obese woman has had 2 months of daily headaches and brief episodes of blurred vision. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilledema, MRI is normal, and lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 32 cm H2O with normal CSF composition. She is started on acetazolamide. Two weeks later she reports tingling in her fingers and around her mouth.
oneliner: 44F + obese + headache + papilledema + normal MRI + opening pressure 32 cm H2O + on acetazolamide + new finger and perioral tingling → most likely lab change?
ask: Which of the following laboratory changes is most likely?

options.C: Hyperkalemia with high anion gap acidosis

whyNot.B: Acetazolamide makes the kidney **lose bicarbonate**, so the blood becomes acidic rather than alkalotic
whyNot.C: Bicarbonate loss is replaced by chloride, so the anion gap stays **normal**, and potassium is lost rather than retained
whyNot.D: Hypercalcemia gives constipation and stones, not **perioral tingling** after starting acetazolamide
whyNot.E: Acetazolamide acts on **proximal tubule bicarbonate**, not magnesium wasting

answer: Hyperchloremic (normal anion gap) metabolic acidosis with hypokalemia
why: **Acetazolamide** inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, so **bicarbonate is lost in the urine** and replaced by chloride, producing a **normal anion gap acidosis**. Potassium is wasted too, and **paresthesias** are a typical effect.

drug.name: Acetazolamide
drug.how: Inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule, so bicarbonate reabsorption falls and urine becomes alkaline with loss of sodium, potassium and water; also lowers CSF and aqueous humor production
drug.use: Idiopathic intracranial hypertension, glaucoma, acute mountain sickness, urinary alkalinization
drug.watch: Hyperchloremic normal anion gap acidosis, hypokalemia, paresthesias, calcium phosphate stones, drowsiness; sulfa allergy

idea.rule: Drugs that block bicarbonate reabsorption cause a normal anion gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis.
also: Topiramate weakly inhibits carbonic anhydrase: acidosis, kidney stones and paresthesias
Acetazolamide for altitude sickness: the acidosis stimulates breathing
Alkaline urine from acetazolamide favors calcium phosphate stones
Diarrhea and renal tubular acidosis are other causes of normal anion gap acidosis

stem: A 62-year-old man with Parkinson disease has taken pramipexole for 8 months. His tremor and rigidity are better controlled, but his wife reports that for the last 3 months he has spent most nights gambling online and has lost much of their savings. He has no psychiatric history, takes no antipsychotic or antidepressant, and has no fever or diarrhea.
oneliner: 62M + Parkinson disease + pramipexole for 8 months + motor symptoms better + 3 months of nightly online gambling + no psychiatric history, antipsychotic, fever or diarrhea → most likely adverse effect?
ask: Which of the following adverse effects of his medication is most likely responsible?

options.A: Tardive dyskinesia of the face and tongue
options.D: Serotonin syndrome with clonus and diarrhea

whyNot.A: Follows chronic dopamine **blockade**, and he takes **no antipsychotic**
whyNot.C: Needs **fever** and severe rigidity; he has **no fever** and his motor symptoms are better
whyNot.D: Needs a serotonergic drug and causes **diarrhea**; he takes **no antidepressant** and has no diarrhea
whyNot.E: Describes motor fluctuations; his **motor symptoms are better controlled** and the problem is gambling

answer: Impulse control disorder (compulsive gambling) from dopamine agonist therapy
why: **New compulsive gambling** in a Parkinson patient on **pramipexole** with no psychiatric history is an **impulse control disorder** from stimulating D2/D3 receptors in the mesolimbic reward pathway. Reducing or stopping the agonist usually resolves it.

drug.name: Pramipexole
drug.how: Directly stimulates D2/D3 receptors in the striatum, replacing missing dopamine without needing conversion
drug.watch: Impulse control disorders (gambling, shopping, hypersexuality), sleep attacks, orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations, leg edema; ergot agonists (bromocriptine, cabergoline) add risk of fibrosis

idea.rule: Dopamine agonists can over-activate the mesolimbic reward pathway, causing compulsive behaviors.
also: Ropinirole causes the same: gambling, shopping, hypersexuality
Pramipexole and ropinirole also cause sleep attacks and orthostatic hypotension
Aripiprazole, a partial D2 agonist, has been linked to compulsive gambling
Management is to reduce or stop the dopamine agonist
Raising the dose can also cause hallucinations and psychosis through the same mesolimbic overstimulation

stem: A 22-year-old woman has had migraine headaches for 6 years, each preceded by about 20 minutes of zigzag lines in the left visual field. Three months ago she started a combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive, and her attacks have increased from once a month to twice a week. She does not smoke, her blood pressure is normal, and she has no abdominal pain, jaundice or family history of cancer.
oneliner: 22F + migraine with visual aura for 6 years + combined oral contraceptive started 3 months ago + attacks now twice a week + nonsmoker, normal BP, no abdominal pain, jaundice or family cancer → main reason to stop?
ask: Which of the following is the main reason to stop this contraceptive?

options.A: Spontaneous rupture of a hepatic adenoma
options.B: Cholestatic jaundice from impaired bile flow
options.D: Higher lifetime risk of invasive breast cancer
options.E: Loss of bone mineral density over years

whyNot.A: Presents with sudden **abdominal pain**, which she does not have
whyNot.B: Would cause **jaundice and itching**; she has neither
whyNot.D: Small risk, and unrelated to her **worsening aura headaches**; she has **no family history of cancer**
whyNot.E: Occurs with long-term injectable progestin, not a reason related to her **aura headaches**

why: **Migraine with aura** is itself linked to ischemic stroke, and **estrogen** adds a prothrombotic effect, so combined hormonal contraceptives are **contraindicated**. Her **worsening attacks** are another warning; switch to an IUD or a progestin-only method.

drug.name: Combined oral contraceptive (ethinyl estradiol plus a progestin)
drug.how: Suppresses GnRH, FSH and LH to prevent ovulation; also thickens cervical mucus and thins the endometrium
drug.use: Contraception, dysmenorrhea, heavy periods, endometriosis, acne and hirsutism in PCOS
drug.watch: Venous thromboembolism and stroke (especially with migraine with aura, smoking after 35, hypertension), hepatic adenoma, cholestasis; contraindicated with prior VTE, breast cancer, active liver disease

idea.rule: Estrogen raises clotting factors, so estrogen-containing contraception is avoided when thrombotic risk is high.
also: Prior DVT or a known thrombophilia such as factor V Leiden
Safe alternatives: copper or levonorgestrel IUD, progestin-only methods
